content: Plasmodium is a genus of parasitic protozoa responsible for causing malaria. The life cycle of Plasmodium involves two hosts: a mosquito vector and a vertebrate host. At least ten species of Plasmodium are known to infect humans, while others infect animals such as birds, reptiles, and rodents. The genus Plasmodium was first described in 1885 by Marchiafava and Celli, and over 175 species have been identified to date. However, the taxonomy of Plasmodium is still under revision, as some related genera, such as Haemocystis and Hepatocystis, appear closely related. It is also likely that other species, such as Haemoproteus meleagridis, may eventually be included in this genus. The host range of Plasmodium is not uniform across mammalian orders. At least 29 species infect non-human primates, while rodent infections are rare outside tropical Africa. A few species infect bats, porcupines, and squirrels, but carnivores, insectivores, and marsupials are not known to serve as hosts. In 1898, Ronald Ross demonstrated the presence of Plasmodium in the midgut wall and salivary glands of Culex mosquitoes, earning him the Nobel Prize in 1902. However, Giovanni Battista Grassi also showed that human malaria is exclusively transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes. While mosquitoes are the primary vectors, other genera such as Culex, Culiceta, Mansonia, and Aedes may also act as vectors for certain species. For human malaria, all known vectors belong to the genus Anopheles, while bird malaria is commonly transmitted by Culex species. Only female mosquitoes bite, as they require blood meals for egg-laying due to the low protein content of nectar. The life cycle of Plasmodium is complex. Sporozoites from the saliva of a biting female mosquito are transmitted to the blood or lymphatic system of the host. These sporozoites migrate to the liver, where they invade hepatocytes and enter a dormant stage called hypnozoites. The transition from the hepatic stage to the erythrocytic stage was unclear until 2006, when it was discovered that the parasite buds off hepatocytes in merosomes containing hundreds or thousands of merozoites. These merosomes lodge in pulmonary capillaries, disintegrating over 48–72 hours to release merozoites. Merozoites invade red blood cells, where they develop into ring-shaped forms, then larger trophozoites, and finally schizonts. Schizonts divide to produce new merozoites, which leave the red blood cells to invade new ones. Some merozoites differentiate into male or female gametocytes, which are taken up by mosquitoes during feeding. In the mosquito midgut, gametocytes develop into gametes, fertilize each other, and form motile zygotes called ookinetes. Ookinetes penetrate the midgut wall, embed on its exterior, and divide to produce sporozoites. These sporozoites migrate to the mosquito's salivary glands, ready to infect the next host. Reactivation of hypnozoites has been reported up to 30 years after the initial infection in humans, though the triggers for reactivation remain unknown. Hypnozoites are known to occur in species such as Plasmodium malariae, Plasmodium ovale, and Plasmodium vivax, but not in Plasmodium falciparum. The evolutionary history of Plasmodium is linked to its adaptation to parasitism. The phylum Apicomplexia, to which Plasmodium belongs, likely originated from photosynthetic dinoflagellates. Over time, these organisms evolved the ability to invade intestinal cells and lost their photosynthetic capabilities. Plasmodium is thought to have evolved from a parasite that initially infected the intestinal wall via the orofecal route and later adapted to infect the liver. Eventually, it developed the ability to infect red blood cells and survive in mosquitoes. Once mosquito transmission was established, the orofecal route was abandoned. Current theories suggest that Plasmodium, Hepatocystis, and Haemoproteus evolved from Leucocytozoon species, which infect white blood cells, liver, and spleen cells and are transmitted by black flies. Plasmodium's ability to invade erythrocytes remains poorly understood, as the process takes less than 30 seconds. The genus is estimated to have evolved around 130 million years ago, coinciding with the rapid spread of flowering plants, which likely increased mosquito populations and their contact with vertebrates. Plasmodium species exhibit a pattern of alternating sexual and asexual reproduction, a common strategy among parasitic organisms. Asexual reproduction is advantageous under stable conditions, as it produces genetically identical offspring well-adapted to the environment. Sexual reproduction, on the other hand, introduces genetic diversity, which is beneficial when adapting to new hosts or stressful conditions. On a molecular level, all examined Plasmodium species have 14 chromosomes, one mitochondrion, and one plastid. The plastid, unlike those in algae, is non-photosynthetic, and its function remains unclear, though it may play a role in reproduction. Plasmodium damages red blood cells using plasmepsin enzymes, which degrade hemoglobin. Diagnostic characteristics of Plasmodium include the formation of gamonts in erythrocytes, merogony in erythrocytes and other tissues, the presence of hemozoin, and the use of mosquitoes or sandflies as vectors. Vertebrate hosts include mammals, birds, and reptiles. Plasmodium belongs to the family Plasmodiidae, order Haemosporidia, and phylum Apicomplexia. There are currently 450 recognized species in this order, though many are undergoing taxonomic revision with DNA analysis. The genus Plasmodium is divided into subgenera based on morphology and host type. For example, the subgenus Laverania includes P. falciparum and P. reichenowi, while the subgenus Plasmodium includes species infecting higher primates. Other subgenera, such as Vinckeia, include species infecting lower primates and other mammals. Avian malaria species are classified into subgenera such as Giovannolaia, Haemamoeba, Huffia, and Novyella. Reptile malaria species are more challenging to classify, with subgenera such as Carinamoeba and Sauroamoeba based on schizont size and host type. The most common Plasmodium species infecting humans are P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae. Additional species capable of infecting humans have been identified using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) techniques. However, some reports of human infections with other Plasmodium species, such as P. eylesi and P. tenue, remain inconclusive. P. falciparum exclusively infects humans, while P. vivax and P. ovale can infect chimpanzees and orangutans. P. ovale's unusual distribution suggests it may be a zoonosis with an unidentified primate host. Other species capable of infecting humans typically have non-human primate hosts. Taxonomy in parasitology has historically been problematic, but DNA-based methods are helping to clarify species relationships.
